© NASA / Ames Research Center — U.S. Government work, public domain. First spacecraft to fly past Saturn (1979-09-01) and the first to image the planet at close range. Used Jupiter's gravity to reach Saturn, demonstrating the gravity-assist technique that would later send Voyager 2 to Uranus and Neptune. Discovered Saturn's F ring + a small inner moon (later resolved by the Voyagers into the co-orbital pair Janus/Epimetheus). Carries the same Pioneer plaque as Pioneer 10. Routine operations ended 1995-09-30 at a heliocentric distance of ~43 AU; the last engineering data arrived 1995-11-24; spacecraft heading toward the constellation Aquila.

Cape Canaveral, 1973-04-06. Launched eight months before Pioneer 10 reached Jupiter — Pioneer 11's primary purpose was to use Jupiter's gravity to reach Saturn ahead of the Voyagers and scout the ring-plane crossing geometry.

Closest approach 42,800 km above the cloud tops on 1974-12-03 — even closer than Pioneer 10. Returns the first images of Jupiter's polar regions and confirms the magnetosphere boundary's response to the solar wind. The flyby bends the trajectory dramatically — slingshot raises the aphelion past Saturn at a high inclination.

Closest approach 20,900 km above Saturn's cloud tops on 1979-09-01 — the first spacecraft to visit Saturn, about 14 months ahead of Voyager 1. Discovered the thin F-ring and a small inner moon (later resolved by the Voyagers into the co-orbital pair Janus/Epimetheus); the ring-plane crossing geometry it tested cleared the Voyagers to attempt the same path. Routine operations ended 1995-09-30; the last engineering data arrived 1995-11-24.
First spacecraft to fly past Saturn (1979-09-01); demonstrated the gravity-assist that sent Voyager 2 onward

Pioneer 11 was the second scout, and it went further than its twin. After its own pass by Jupiter it used the planet’s gravity to cross the solar system and reach Saturn in 1979 — the first spacecraft ever to do so — deliberately flying through the ring plane to test whether the region was safe. It found the gap the Voyagers would thread a year later. Much of what made the Grand Tour possible was this: a small, cheap probe sent ahead to take the risks and map the hazards, so the flagships behind it could fly with confidence instead of fear.

Twin of Pioneer 10, launched a year later. Pioneer 11 used Jupiter’s gravity to bend its trajectory toward Saturn — the canonical proof of gravity-assist propulsion, the technique that later enabled the Voyager Grand Tour. At Saturn it discovered the F ring and a small inner moon later resolved into the co-orbital pair Janus/Epimetheus. Carries the same Pioneer plaque as its twin. Routine operations ended 1995-09-30 at a heliocentric distance of ~43 AU; the last engineering data arrived 1995-11-24; the spacecraft is now heading toward the constellation Aquila.
